project.name: Panbride
project.boundarySource: Mapped named-place location with a conservative editorial study buffer
project.researchNotes: Full strict-boundary audit. All 20 local HES/NRHE records are retained. Eleven defensibly dated records are visible; two dated external-buffer records and seven undated records are map-hidden. The score is not inherited from Carnoustie facilities. Angus-wide full audit completed 2026-09-01: all six visitor categories, the four named commercial trail providers, current official/conventional routes, strict-boundary scoring and local HES/NRHE integrity were checked.

touristAppeal.label: Selector only
touristAppeal.summary: Panbride has a rewarding churchyard group and Craigmill Den on a verified council walk, but it remains a very small hamlet without a café, public toilet, picnic facility or dedicated visitor car park. These attractions support a worthwhile local detour, not a 60+ town destination.
touristAppeal.dogAccessSummary: The den walk is suitable for controlled dogs, with care on roads, around livestock and in the churchyard.

townGuide.characterTag: Historic Angus hamlet beside Craigmill Den
townGuide.headline: A churchyard-and-den detour rather than a full destination
townGuide.intro: Panbride scores 54% and remains selector-only. Its church group and the official Craigmill Den walk are worthwhile, but practical visitor infrastructure belongs chiefly to neighbouring Carnoustie.

features.licence: Open Government Licence v3.0; retain Historic Environment Scotland attribution.
features.reviewNotes: Retained from the local HES statutory layer. Hidden until a defensible historic period is documented.
features.fullDescription: The monument comprises the remains of two enclosed settlements and associated features of prehistoric date represented by cropmarks visible on oblique aerial photographs. The monument lies in arable farmland at around 25m OD. It comprises the remains of two enclosed settlements both measuring some 50m by 50m within ditches some 1.5-2m wide. Within and around the enclosures are a series of cropmarks some of which are also likely to be archaeological in origin, representing buildings, pits and souterrains (semi-underground storage structures) associated with the settlement. The area to be scheduled encompasses the principal cropmarks described above and an area around them in which traces of associated activity may be expected to survive. It is an irregular quadrilateral with maximum dimensions of 220m NNW-SSE by 120m as marked in red on the accompanying map.

features.licence: Open Government Licence v3.0; retain Historic Environment Scotland attribution.
features.reviewNotes: Retained from the local HES statutory layer. Hidden until a defensible historic period is documented.
features.fullDescription: The monument comprises the remains of a fort of later prehistoric date represented by cropmarks visible on oblique aerial photographs. The monument lies in arable farmland at around 25m OD. The D-shaped fort consists of two concentric ramparts, the ditches of which measure about 2m (outer) and 4m (inner) wide, enclosing an area some 100m across. The W edge of the fort is defined by the adjacent Craigmill Burn. The area to be scheduled encompasses the cropmark remains and an area around them in which traces of associated activity may be expected to survive. It is irregular in shape with maximum dimensions of 130m N-S by 80m as marked in red on the accompanying map.
